## Skill Codification Rule ("Asked Twice = Failure")

No one-off judgment work. If the user asks for something that will need to happen again, the agent must:

1. Do it manually the first time on 3–10 items.
2. Show the output to the user.
3. If the user approves, codify it as a parameterized skill in `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (judgment work) or `.claude/commands/<name>.md` (slash-invocable workflow). If the task is deterministic and time-driven, also register a cron entry per the Script Automation Rule.
4. Re-run the new skill once to verify it reproduces the approved output.

**Test:** If the user has to ask for the same thing twice without it being a one-line skill invocation, the agent failed. Document repeating patterns in `SKILL.md` files, not in chat scrollback.

**Skill shape:** Skill files are parameterized procedures, not domain scripts. A skill describes the process; the invocation supplies the world (TARGET, KIND, DATASET, ROLE). Four near-identical skills with different filenames is a smell — collapse them into one skill with arguments.

The LUT doctorate (4 years, 2027–2030) and the DWS IQ version roadmap

### 24.5 Governance

- `/truth-check` external claims before send; apply the Brand Standard for voice.

- Enforcement: an important message that was sent but not saved is an institutional-memory loss — treat as a Rule 12 violation.

## 25. Universal Document Footer (mandatory)

Every document produced in this repository — internal or external, narrative or tabular — **must** carry a footer block at the **bottom** of the document containing four elements:

1. **Document version** — equal to the §2 header version (lockstep; never a different number).
2. **Date** — the content date (DD.MM.YYYY). If the file is a repository copy of an externally-authored/exported artifact, also note the repo-copy date.
3. **Copyright** — `© <year> Lifetime Oy (Y-tunnus 0772407-9). All rights reserved.`
4. **Business Confidentiality clause** — unless the document is explicitly classified **Public** (see §23.2).

### 25.1 Canonical footer block

```
***

**Document version:** vX.Y · **Date:** DD.MM.YYYY · **Owner:** Lifetime Oy
© <year> Lifetime Oy (Y-tunnus 0772407-9). All rights reserved.
**Business Confidential.** This document contains confidential and proprietary information of Lifetime Oy. It is disclosed solely to the intended recipient under an applicable NDA or business relationship and may not be copied, distributed, or disclosed to any third party without Lifetime Oy's prior written consent.
```

### 25.2 Rules

- **Version lockstep.** The footer version must always equal the header (§2) version. Bump both in the same edit — a mismatch is a Rule 12 (fail-loud) violation.
- **Public documents** replace the confidentiality clause with a short public-license/attribution line, but still carry version, date, and copyright.
- **Customer-facing documents (§20.6)** already move the version block + copyright to the end — this footer _is_ that block; do not duplicate it at the top for those docs.
- **Whitepapers (§23.1)** carry the per-page printed footer defined there; §25 is the Markdown-source equivalent and both must agree on classification.
- **Delimiter:** the footer opens with `***` (never `---`) per the Markdown Delimiter Rule.

## 26. Repository-First, Then Export (anti-drift)

A Google Doc, Drive file, PDF, Gamma deck, `.docx`, or `.xlsx` that has **no repository source-of-truth file** is a data-drift incident, not a deliverable. Exports are generated copies; the repository `.md` (or `.csv` for tabular models) is the master.

### 26.1 Order of operations (required)

1. **Traceability** - Every document must be traceable to its creator and session
2. **Versioning** - All documents must have clear version history
3. **Consistency** - Same format across all document types
4. **Bilingual** - Support for both English and Finnish
5. **Automation-Friendly** - Machine-readable metadata

---

## 2. Document Header Standard

### 2.1 Required Header Block

**ALL documents MUST include this header block at the top:**

> **IMPORTANT: Pandoc Compatibility.** Use `***` (not `---`) as delimiters around
> the VERSION AND AGENT HISTORY block. Pandoc interprets `---` as YAML front matter,
> which causes parse errors because the history block isn't valid YAML.
> Both `***` and `---` render as horizontal rules in markdown, but only `---` triggers
> YAML parsing.

```markdown
# [Document Title]

---

# VERSION AND AGENT HISTORY

Version: X.Y

Sessions & Modifications:

- Version: X.Y | Tool: [Tool Name] | Session: [Session ID] | Date: DD.MM.YYYY | Changes: [Description]

Session Links & References:

- [Tool Name] ([Session ID]): [GitHub commit link]
- View on GitHub: [Document link]

Document Status:

- Created: DD.MM.YYYY
- Last Modified: DD.MM.YYYY
- Language: [Primary Language]
- Languages Available: [List]
- Publication Status: [ACTIVE / DRAFT / OUTDATED / ARCHIVED / DEPRECATED]

---
```

### 2.2 Header Components

| Component               | Required       | Description               | Example                                     |
| ----------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Version**             | ✅ Yes         | Semantic version (X.Y)    | `1.0`, `1.1`, `2.0`                         |
| **Tool**                | ✅ Yes         | AI tool or author         | `Cursor AI`, `Claude Code`, `Manual`        |
| **Session**             | ✅ Yes         | Unique session identifier | `2025-12-30`, `QVvDX`, `IjtD0`              |
| **Date**                | ✅ Yes         | Date of modification      | `30.12.2025`                                |
| **Changes**             | ✅ Yes         | Brief description         | `Initial creation`, `Added workflow naming` |
| **Session Links**       | ⚠️ Recommended | GitHub commit links       | URL to commits                              |
| **Created**             | ✅ Yes         | Document creation date    | `30.12.2025`                                |
| **Last Modified**       | ✅ Yes         | Last modification date    | `30.12.2025`                                |
| **Language**            | ✅ Yes         | Primary language          | `English`, `Finnish`, `Bilingual`           |
| **Languages Available** | ✅ Yes         | All available languages   | `English, Suomi`                            |
| **Publication Status**  | ✅ Yes         | Document status           | `ACTIVE`, `DRAFT`, `OUTDATED`, `ARCHIVED`   |

### 2.3 Publication Status Values

Use plain text status labels. Emoji icons are optional (display only).

| Status           | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **ACTIVE**       | Document is current and in use                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **DRAFT**        | Document is work in progress                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **OUTDATED**     | Document is superseded, no longer maintained — pending archive                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **ARCHIVED**     | Document is in `docs/archive/`, kept for historical reference                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **DEPRECATED**   | Document is outdated and should not be used                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **UNDER REVIEW** | Document is being reviewed                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **FINAL**        | Customer-facing deliverable (§20.6 scope) that is complete, corrected, and ready to send/submit — used in place of ACTIVE for one-shot external deliverables (CVs, bid attachments, offers) that are not part of a maintained internal lifecycle |

> **Pandoc note:** Avoid emoji in publication status if generating PDF via LaTeX.
> HTML engine handles emoji fine. Use text labels (`ACTIVE`, `DRAFT`, etc.) as the
> canonical value; emoji is decorative.

### 2.4 Document Lifecycle

Documents follow this lifecycle:

```
DRAFT → ACTIVE → OUTDATED → ARCHIVED
```

# Copilot Instructions for DWS6

## Project Overview

**DWS IQ 6** is an enterprise-grade industrial climate intelligence and compliance platform for EU-regulated industries. It automates climate compliance (Fit for 55, ETS, CBAM, CSRD) across 25+ EU industries.

**Repository size:** ~500+ files, TypeScript/JavaScript/Python polyglot codebase  
**Main languages:** TypeScript 5.9, Python 3.11+, React 19.2  
**Target runtime:** Node.js 20+, Python 3.11+

## Build, Test, and Validation (CRITICAL - Always Follow This Sequence)

### First Time Setup
```bash
# 1. ALWAYS install dependencies first (required before any build/test)
npm install

# 2. Copy environment template (if .env doesn't exist)
cp .env.example .env

# 3. THEN build TypeScript
npm run build

# 4. Verify tests pass
npm test
```

**IMPORTANT:** Build will fail with TypeScript errors if you run `npm run build` before `npm install`. Always install dependencies first.

### Development Workflow
```bash
# Start backend with hot reload (PREFERRED for development)
npm run dev              # Uses tsx watch - auto-reloads on changes

# Build TypeScript (for production)
npm run build           # Compiles to dist/ directory

# Run tests (Vitest)
npm test                # Unit and integration tests
npm run test:ui         # Interactive test UI

# No linter configured yet - eslint pending setup
npm run lint            # Currently just echoes "No linter configured"
```

### Python Scripts (Firehorse/)
```bash
# Install Python dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Security scanning tools
pip install -r requirements-security.txt

# Development tools
pip install -r dev-requirements.txt

# Python linting with Ruff (replaces Black, Flake8)
ruff check .                    # Fast linting
ruff format .                   # Code formatting
bandit -r Firehorse/           # Security scanning
safety check                    # Dependency vulnerability scan
```

### Frontend Dashboard (dws6.com/dashboard/firehorse/v9-react/)
```bash
cd dws6.com/dashboard/firehorse/v9-react/
npm install
npm run dev              # Vite dev server on port 5173
npm run build            # Production build
```

## Repository Architecture

### Key Directories
```
/
├── src/                          # Backend Express API (TypeScript)
│   ├── app.ts                    # Main Express app entry point
│   ├── routes/                   # API route handlers
│   ├── middleware/               # Auth, validation, error handling
│   ├── services/                 # Business logic (email, AI, Redis)
│   ├── integrations/             # ERP (SAP, IFS) & ESG integrations
│   ├── mcp/                      # Model Context Protocol implementation
│   └── __tests__/                # Vitest test files
├── dws6.com/dashboard/           # Frontend dashboards
│   └── firehorse/v9-react/       # Main React dashboard (Vite + Tailwind)
├── Firehorse/                    # Python product suite
│   ├── Report/                   # Analytics engine
│   ├── Automation/               # Python automation scripts
│   ├── ContentMS/                # Content management
│   └── Omnichannel/              # Multi-channel outreach
├── landing-pages/                # Next.js/Cloudflare Pages sites
│   ├── dws6-com/                 # Production landing pages
│   ├── dws10-com/                # DWS 10 landing pages
│   └── onelifetime-world/        # Lifetime landing pages
├── mcp-hub/                      # MCP orchestration platform
├── mcp-servers/                  # Individual MCP server implementations
├── supabase/migrations/          # Database schema migrations
├── .github/workflows/            # 18 CI/CD workflows
├── scripts/                      # Build, deployment, automation scripts
└── public/                       # Static assets served by Express
```

### Configuration Files
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript compiler config (strict mode)
- `vitest.config.ts` - Vitest test runner config
- `pyproject.toml` - Python project config (Ruff, Bandit)
- `.env.example` - Environment variable template (144+ vars)
- `.gitignore` - CRITICAL: Prevents committing secrets, node_modules, etc.

## CI/CD Pipelines (18 GitHub Actions Workflows)

Located in `.github/workflows/` - these run automatically on PRs and commits:

**Critical workflows that must pass:**
1. `security-check-pr.yml` - Security scans (runs on all PRs)
2. `deploy-pilot.yml` - Deployment to pilot environment
3. `deploy-scaleway.yml` - Primary production deployment
4. `morning-briefing.yml` - Scheduled email automation

**Before committing:** Ensure your changes won't break these workflows. Common failures:
- Missing environment variables in code
- TypeScript compilation errors (run `npm run build` first)
- Test failures (run `npm test` first)
- Security vulnerabilities (check with `bandit` for Python)

## Code Style and Conventions

### TypeScript
- **Strict TypeScript:** No `any` types, prefer `unknown` for dynamic data
- **Validation:** Use Zod schemas for runtime validation (not just TypeScript types)
- **Interfaces:** Define interfaces for all API contracts
- **Naming:** 
  - Files: `kebab-case.ts` (utils), `PascalCase.tsx` (React components)
  - Variables: `camelCase`
  - Constants: `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`
  - Types/Interfaces: `PascalCase`

### React (v9-react dashboard)
- Functional components with hooks (no class components)
- TailwindCSS for styling (no inline styles or CSS-in-JS)
- Co-locate components with their styles
- Use Zod for form validation

### Python (Firehorse/)
- Follow PEP 8 (enforced by Ruff)
- Use type hints (enforced by mypy in pyproject.toml)
- **Security:** Use `simpleeval` library's `simple_eval()` for formula evaluation, NEVER use `eval()` or `ast.literal_eval()`
- Add `# nosec` comments only for verified false positives

### Email Rules (CRITICAL)
- **NEVER use `noreply@` addresses** - all emails must be replyable
- Default sender: `risto@onelifetime.world` (verified in Amazon SES and Resend.com)
- Default recipient: `risto@lifetime.fi`
- Delivery: SMTP (SES) primary, Resend fallback. Pattern: `process.env.EMAIL_FROM || 'risto@onelifetime.world'`

## Security (NEVER COMMIT SECRETS)

### Prohibited Actions
- ❌ Commit secrets, API keys, passwords to any file
- ❌ Commit PII or customer data (GDPR violation)
- ❌ Skip input validation on user inputs
- ❌ Use `git add -f Admin/` or force-add ignored files
- ❌ Use `eval()` or `exec()` with user-provided strings
- ❌ Force push to main/master branches

### Required Actions
- ✅ Use environment variables for ALL secrets (see `.env.example`)
- ✅ Validate all inputs with express-validator or Zod
- ✅ Use parameterized queries (never string concatenation for SQL)
- ✅ Write tests for security-critical code
- ✅ Run security scans before committing (`bandit`, `safety`)

### .gitignore Patterns (VERIFIED)
These patterns prevent accidental secret commits:
```gitignore
.env*                    # All environment files
*.secret, *.key, *.pem   # Secret files
node_modules/            # Dependencies
__pycache__/             # Python cache
dist/, build/            # Build artifacts
*.log, logs/             # May contain sensitive data
```

**Before every commit:** Run `git status` to verify no `.env` or secret files are staged.

## Common Pitfalls and Workarounds

### Issue: TypeScript Build Fails with "Cannot find name 'process'"
**Cause:** Missing @types/node dependency  
**Fix:** Ensure `npm install` was run first. The error appears if you build before installing dependencies.

### Issue: Morning Briefing Runs Twice During DST Transitions
**Cause:** GitHub Actions cron uses UTC, Finland observes DST  
**Fix:** Use dual cron entries with time-guard in script (see `.github/workflows/morning-briefing.yml:6-11`)

### Issue: node-cron Doesn't Work in Serverless (Cloud Run, Scaleway)
**Cause:** In-process schedulers incompatible with scale-to-zero platforms  
**Fix:** Use external triggers (GitHub Actions, Cloud Scheduler) instead of in-process cron

### Issue: ML/DS Pipeline Artifacts Appear in Git Status
**Cause:** Generated files not in .gitignore  
**Fix:** These patterns are already in .gitignore (lines 104-110):
```gitignore
reports/figures/*.png
reports/*.json
models/*.pkl
data/raw_dataset.csv
data/cleaned_dataset.csv
```
Never commit these runtime artifacts.

## Testing Guidance

### Test Structure
```
src/__tests__/           # Vitest tests co-located with source
├── auth.test.ts         # Authentication tests
├── bim-routes.test.ts   # BIM API endpoint tests
└── security/            # Security-specific tests
```

### Writing Tests
```typescript
// ALWAYS mock auth middleware to avoid JWT_SECRET requirements
import { vi } from 'vitest';

// Mock BEFORE imports
vi.mock('../middleware/auth.middleware.js', () => ({
  authenticateJWT: vi.fn((req, res, next) => next())
}));

// THEN import routes (after mock)
const { default: router } = await import('../routes/bim.routes.js');
```

### Running Tests
```bash
npm test                # Run all tests
npm test -- --watch     # Watch mode
npm test -- --coverage  # Coverage report (aim for >80%)
npm run test:ui         # Interactive UI
```

## Git Workflow

### Branch Naming
- `claude/<feature>-<session-id>` - AI-assisted work (e.g., `claude/auth-fix-abc123`)
- `feature/<name>` - Human-developed features
- `fix/<description>` - Bug fixes

### Commit Messages
```
<type>: <description>

Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore

Example:
feat: add BIM emission factor validation endpoint
```

## Deployment

**Primary:** Scaleway Serverless Containers (fr-par, Paris, France)  
**Edge:** Cloudflare Workers/Pages (dws6.com, dws10.com)  
**Database:** Supabase (EU-hosted, PostgreSQL + pgvector)  
**AI Inference:** Groq API (Llama 3.1 70B), Claude Sonnet 4.5

**Deployment trigger:** Push to `main` branch runs `.github/workflows/deploy-scaleway.yml`

## Automated PR Workflow (HIL Automation)

This repo uses a fully automated multi-agent PR workflow that **replaces manual human-in-the-loop review**.

### Flow
1. **Claude Code** generates implementation on a feature branch and opens a draft PR
2. **AI Code Review (HIL)** workflow triggers automatically (`.github/workflows/ai-pr-review.yml`)
   - **Claude** does quick sanity check (security, correctness, breaking changes)
   - **Gemini** does deep HIL review (replaces human reviewer: edge cases, tests, architecture, security audit)
   - Both must approve — Gemini is the mandatory quality gate
   - Posts combined review as PR comment
   - Adds labels: `ai-reviewed` + `ai-approved` or `ai-changes-requested`
3. **If changes requested** (mandatory, not optional): Gemini's required changes + test gaps are formatted as structured @copilot instructions
   - Copilot coding agent picks up the comment and implements fixes autonomously
   - Pushes to the PR branch, re-triggering the review workflow
   - Loop repeats until both reviewers approve (typically 1-3 iterations)
4. **Gemini requests fixes → Copilot implements** (mandatory, not optional): This is the core automation loop
   - Gemini acts as strict senior engineer — flags critical issues, missing tests, edge cases
   - Fix instructions are specific and actionable (file:line references)
   - Copilot implements changes, runs `npm run build` and `npm test`
   - Review re-triggers automatically on push
5. **When approved**: `ai-approved` label triggers auto-merge workflow
   - Verifies all CI checks pass
   - Enables squash auto-merge (or adds `ready-to-merge` label)
6. **Human override**: Add `do-not-merge` or `needs-human-review` labels to pause

### Copilot Coding Agent
- Setup steps defined in `.github/copilot-setup-steps.yml`
- Copilot agent runs `npm install`, installs Python tools, builds TypeScript
- When tagged in PR comments, it implements requested changes autonomously

### Gemini MCP Integration
- Gemini MCP server is registered in `mcp-hub/server.py` (currently disabled, port 8768)
- The PR review workflow uses Gemini API directly via `GOOGLE_AI_API_KEY` secret
- Model: `gemini-2.0-flash` (fast, strong on code critique)

| `ai-reviewed` | AI review has been performed (dual-model) |
| `ai-approved` | Both Claude + Gemini approved |
| `ai-changes-requested` | One or both reviewers found issues |
| `ready-to-merge` | All checks passed, safe to merge |
| `do-not-merge` | Blocks auto-merge (human override) |

## 2. Lifetime Scope Signals Protocol

### What Are Lifetime Scope Signals?

Signals are the communication mechanism between agents. When an agent completes a milestone, it **emits** a signal. Other agents **listen** for signals before proceeding with dependent tasks.

### Signal Format

```
[AGENT-XX]:SIGNAL_TYPE:MILESTONE:TIMESTAMP
```

**Components:**

- `AGENT-XX`: Agent identifier (e.g., `AGENT-01`, `AGENT-07`)
- `SIGNAL_TYPE`: `READY`, `COMPLETE`, `ERROR`, `BLOCKED`
- `MILESTONE`: Specific deliverable (e.g., `supabase-auth`, `rls-policies`)
- `TIMESTAMP`: ISO 8601 format

**Examples:**

```
[AGENT-07]:READY:rls-policies:2026-01-05T14:30:00Z
[AGENT-01]:COMPLETE:v1-auth:2026-01-10T09:00:00Z
[AGENT-02]:BLOCKED:report-api:2026-01-06T10:15:00Z
```

### Signal Types

| Type       | Meaning                                          | Action                               |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `READY`    | Milestone achieved, dependent agents can proceed | Unblocks downstream agents           |
| `COMPLETE` | All agent work finished                          | Agent moves to complete status       |
| `ERROR`    | Agent encountered failure                        | Alerts coordinator, may block others |
| `BLOCKED`  | Agent waiting for external dependency            | No action until unblocked            |

### How Agents Learn Signals

#### Option A: File-Based (Current Implementation)

Agents read from `AGENT_SIGNAL_REGISTRY.json`:

```javascript
// coordinator.cjs
const registry = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("AGENT_SIGNAL_REGISTRY.json"));
const myDependencies = registry.agents["agent-02"].signals.listening;
const emittedSignals = collectEmittedSignals(registry);
const unmet = myDependencies.filter((sig) => !emittedSignals.has(sig));
// If unmet.length === 0, agent can proceed
```

**Commands:**

```bash
cd .workflows/agents
node coordinator.cjs status    # Show all agent statuses
node coordinator.cjs signals   # Show signal log
node coordinator.cjs ready     # Show which agents can launch
node coordinator.cjs emit agent-07 READY:schema-users  # Emit signal
```

#### Option B: MCP Hub Real-Time (Future)

```python
# mcp-hub/server.py addition
@app.post("/signals/emit")
async def emit_signal(agent_id: str, signal: str):
    await supabase.table("agent_signals").insert({...})
    await notify_listeners(agent_id, signal)
```

mode: "silent_pilot"

```

### Proactive Agents — Observe → Act (Code Wiring)

The deployment phases above are now enforced in the TypeScript agent runtime via
`AgentConfig.autonomyPhase` (`silent_pilot` | `advisor` | `autonomous`, default
`silent_pilot`). The "observe → act" loop is implemented by:

| Concern                                                    | Module                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| What to watch + 2×2 "worth interrupting" gate              | `src/agents/signal-catalogue.ts`           |
| Phase ladder + comparison                                  | `src/agents/autonomy.ts`                   |
| Nudge chokepoint (dedup, rate limit, escalation, delivery) | `src/agents/nudge.service.ts`              |
| Background observation cron + escalation sweep             | `src/agents/signal-poller.ts`              |
| Confirm / Override / Dismiss / Investigate handling        | `src/agents/nudge-response-handler.ts`     |
| `send_notification` agent tool (KYA phase-gated, BLUE)     | `src/agents/tools.ts`                      |
| Persisted nudge state                                      | `supabase/migrations/069_agent_nudges.sql` |

**Currently promoted to Phase 2 (advisor):** `sitesense`, `compliance`,
`customer-sat`. All other agents remain `silent_pilot` and cannot send nudges.

**Guardrails:** an agent below `advisor` is refused `send_notification` at the
tool gate; nudges are deduplicated per `(orgId, signalKey, entityId)` while
pending, rate-limited per agent (default 5/hour, 20/day, counted from the
persisted table so limits hold across instances), and escalated after a 4h
no-response window via the poller's restart-safe `escalate_at` sweep.

## 8. Managed Agent Backends — Claude Managed Agents vs. DGX Managed Agents

**Terminology.** Two execution substrates exist (or are being evaluated) for running DWS agent workloads:

- **Claude Managed Agents** — Anthropic's hosted agent-execution service (public beta as of this writing, `managed-agents-2026-04-01`). Anthropic runs the session/sandbox/tool loop on its own infrastructure; DWS sends events and receives results. Distinct from the raw Messages API, the Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`, self-hosted loop), and the Claude Agent SDK (self-hosted library) — see Anthropic documentation for the full surface comparison.
- **DGX Managed Agents** (this repo's term for the existing self-hosted substrate) — the Godagent architecture (`docs/Deputy-Agents-Architecture.md`) running on DGX Spark hardware (Acer Veriton GN100, NVIDIA GB10 Superchip, `docs/CLOUD_ENVIRONMENTS.md` §3.2.2), Docker + Dockerode container isolation per tenant/agent, Qwen 2.5 72B primary LLM with Claude Haiku fallback via LiteLLM, orchestrated through `infrastructure/dgx-spark/docker-compose.yml` and the `cron` / `ollama-spark` skills. This is already the platform's primary 24/7 runtime (`Cron-works.md`: 31 daily + 16 weekly jobs).

### 8.1 Comparison

| Dimension                  | Claude Managed Agents                                                                                                               | DGX Managed Agents (current)                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hosting / control plane    | Anthropic-run cloud sandbox by default; a self-hosted-worker mode exists but orchestration still lives on Anthropic's control plane | Fully self-hosted: Docker/Dockerode on Lifetime Oy premises                                                                                    |
| Data residency / CLOUD Act | Tool input/output transits Anthropic's control plane even in self-hosted-worker mode; no confirmed EU-only execution SLA found      | Zero CLOUD Act exposure — Finland premises, `--network none` per container, tenant LWM stays on host (§5, Deputy-Agents-Architecture.md)       |
| Marginal cost              | Standard token rates **+ a per-session-hour execution surcharge** — see uncertainty flag below                                      | Zero marginal compute cost once hardware is owned; only power draw + occasional Claude fallback tokens                                         |
| Sandbox / tool surface     | Bash, Read/Write/Edit, Glob/Grep, web fetch/search out of the box; custom tools via JSON schema; MCP connector support              | Discrete, typed tools only (`tools.ts`) — deliberately no general `execute_code`, per AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES §11.4 (KYA / lethal-trifecta gating) |
| Model flexibility          | Claude models only (Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5)                                                                                | Multi-model: Qwen 2.5 72B primary, Claude fallback, DeepSeek/Mistral Enterprise override, per-tenant fine-tuned LWMs                           |
| Statefulness / audit       | Native multi-turn session persistence, managed memory tool                                                                          | `agent_executions` / `agent_loop_iterations` (Supabase/Aiven) + hash-chain audit for EU AI Act Article 12                                      |
| Ops burden                 | ~Zero — Anthropic manages scaling, patching, sandbox lifecycle                                                                      | Ours — container lifecycle, zombie cleanup, VRAM budget (128GB GB10, max 2 models loaded), heartbeat monitoring                                |
| Maturity / risk            | Public beta — event schema, limits, and pricing may still shift                                                                     | Production — already load-bearing for the platform's scheduled work                                                                            |

EU data-residency posture is similarly unconfirmed from public docs as of this writing.

### 8.2 What each is actually good for

- **Claude Managed Agents fits:** short-lived, non-regulated, non-sovereignty-sensitive workloads where standing up local infra isn't worth it — e.g. the sales/marketing agents already exempt from the Ledger-Native Output Contract (`competitor-surveillance`, `seo-audit`, `lead-feedback`, `customer-sat`; see §2 of `AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES.md`), ad hoc research spikes, or overflow capacity when DGX Spark's VRAM budget is saturated (max 2 models concurrent, §5.5 Deputy-Agents-Architecture.md).
- **DGX Managed Agents fits (and stays default) for:** any agent whose output touches the carbon ledger or a customer's regulatory exposure (the non-exempt list in AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES §2), anything requiring EU-sovereign / CLOUD-Act-free execution, anything needing a tenant LWM or a BYO-agent via A2A/MCP, and all 24/7 scheduled work already living on DGX Spark cron.

This mirrors the standing decision already recorded for Firehorse Dreaming (`.claude/clawdbot/memory/clawdbot-architecture.md`): keep the local/DGX substrate as source of truth, and treat Claude Managed Agents as an optional thin adapter — not a migration target — until a concrete gap forces the question.

### 8.3 Implementation Plan

**Phase 0 — Decision gate (no code).**

1. Verify Claude Managed Agents pricing and EU-residency posture directly against Anthropic's current docs/console. Until done, treat the cost/residency rows in §8.1 as provisional.
2. Confirm the sales-agent exemption list (§2 AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES) is the right pilot scope — these agents already don't touch the carbon ledger, so a pilot there carries the least compliance risk.

**Phase 1 — Pilot (one exempt agent).**

1. Pick one exempt, Tier-1 (read-only) agent — e.g. `seo-audit` or `lead-feedback` — as the pilot.
2. Add a `runtime: 'dgx' | 'claude-managed'` field to that agent's `AgentConfig` (`src/agents/types.ts`), defaulting to `'dgx'`.
3. Implement a thin adapter (`src/agents/runtime/managed-agents-client.ts`) wrapping the Managed Agents session API behind the same `execute()` contract `BaseAgent` already returns, so `AgentResponse` shape and downstream consumers (dashboards, `agent_executions` logging) are unaffected.
4. Extend `agent_executions` with a logged `runtime` field via a dedicated migration (not a silent schema change) so both runtimes log identically.
5. Run the pilot for two weeks side-by-side with the DGX version of the same agent; compare cost, latency, and output quality before drawing conclusions.

**Phase 2 — Guardrails before any wider rollout.**

1. Ledger-Native Output Contract (AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES §2): Claude Managed Agents runtime is **not** permitted for any non-exempt agent until Article 12 lineage (`signedBy: SovereigntyLayerSignature`) can be produced from a Managed Agents session — this needs its own design, not an assumption.
2. KYA: a Managed-Agents-backed agent is governed like a BYO agent — it must pass the same `KYACheck` gate (`docs/Deputy-Agents-Architecture.md` §8.3) before promotion past Tier 1 autonomy.
3. Cost tracking: add `claude_managed_agents` to the `model_costs` block (AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES §6) once real pricing is confirmed (Phase 0.1), with its own `budget_monthly_eur` cap separate from direct API spend.
4. Only update `Cron-works.md` / `skills/cron/SKILL.md` failover tiers if a _scheduled_ (not ad hoc) job moves to Managed Agents — no scheduled job is currently a pilot candidate.

**Phase 3 — Scale decision (data-driven, not calendar-driven).**

Only after Phase 1 produces real cost/latency numbers: decide whether Claude Managed Agents becomes a standing overflow tier for exempt agents (burst capacity when DGX Spark's queue/VRAM is saturated) or gets shelved. Do not pre-build multi-agent Managed Agents routing before that data exists (Rule 2 — simplicity first).

**Explicitly out of scope for Managed Agents (stays on DGX by design):** all Godagent/industry-specialist agents (`src/agents/workflow/industry/`), every agent on the non-exempt Ledger-Native list, and all DGX Spark cron-scheduled jobs — sovereignty, cost, and the existing Article 12 audit chain all argue against moving these.

## Core Principle

Ship reliable outcomes fast, but never past security, compliance, or source-of-truth rules.

## Agent Response Format (HIC-Facing Output)

Chat output is for the HIC to **decide and act**, not to watch the agent think.

**Every response carries only these, in this order. Omit any that is empty.**

1. **Decisions** — what was decided or changed, one line each. State the choice, not the deliberation.
2. **Facts used** — the evidence a decision rests on, with its source (`file:line`, commit, URL, or "HIC, <date>"). A fact with no source is marked `unverified`.
3. **HIC actions** — a numbered list of what the human must **get** (credential, access, key, approval) or **do** (deploy, revoke, confirm). Each line: the action, and what breaks without it. If nothing is needed, say "No HIC action."

**Never in chat output:**

- Narration of reasoning, plans, or what is about to be done next.
- Restating what a file, test, or command already says.
- Recapping work already reported earlier in the session.
- Process description ("I checked X, then Y, then found Z") — report Z.
- Apologies, self-assessment, or hedging about the agent's own performance.

**Length.** Default ceiling: 10 lines. A table or code block does not count toward it. Exceed it only when the HIC asked for a document, a draft, or a copy-paste deliverable.

**Act, don't delegate.** Before listing something as an HIC action, verify the agent genuinely cannot do it — check the available tools first. A task handed over that the agent could have completed is a failure, not caution. Reserve HIC actions for things needing credentials the agent lacks, or that are irreversible or outward-facing.

**Detail belongs in files, not chat.** Rationale → `context/`. What happened → `docs/field-notes/`. What changed → `CHANGELOG.md`. Chat points at them; it does not reproduce them.

## Engineering Discipline — The 12 Rules

**Canonical source.** This is the single home for the 12 engineering-discipline rules. Every agent — Claude Code sessions, subagents, `src/agents/` BaseAgent classes, MCP tools, AgentFoundry, and dev-fleet agents — must have access to these and operate by them. They are surfaced at runtime by `.claude/hooks/session-start.sh`, restated for code agents in `AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES.md` (§0), referenced from `AGENTS.md`, and enforced where mechanizable by the hooks in `.claude/hooks/` (see `.claude/hooks/README.md`). Do not fork or paraphrase this list elsewhere — point back here.

1. **Think before coding.** State assumptions explicitly; do not guess. The model cannot read your mind — surface what you are assuming before you act.
2. **Simplicity first.** Minimum code, no speculative abstractions. Reject "for future flexibility" additions — they are next quarter's deletions. (Reinforces `/simplify`.)
3. **Surgical changes.** Touch only what the task requires. Do not improve adjacent code; unrelated refactors blow up review scope. (Mirrors Non-Negotiable Rule 9.)
4. **Goal-driven execution.** Define success criteria upfront and loop until verified. Without an explicit done-condition an agent either loops forever or stops too early. (Use `/goal`, the verification-gate.)
5. **Use the model only for judgment calls** — classification, drafting, summarization, extraction. NOT routing, retries, status-code handling, or deterministic transforms. If code can answer, code answers.
6. **Token budgets are not advisory.** Per-task 4000, per-session 30000 (`CLAUDE_AUTO_MODE_BUDGET`). Past these, agents re-suggest fixes already rejected. Stop, checkpoint, re-scope.
7. **Surface conflicts, don't average them.** Two patterns in the codebase? Pick one and say why. Blending them swallows errors twice.
8. **Read before you write.** Read exports, callers, and shared utilities first, so you reuse instead of duplicating an identical function you never opened.
9. **Tests verify intent, not just behavior.** A test that cannot fail when business logic changes is wrong. All tests can pass while a function returns a constant — assert the intent.
10. **Checkpoint every significant step.** Commit/verify before building the next step, so step 6 is never stacked on a broken step 4. (Backed by `/ship`, session-stop governance.)
11. **Match the codebase conventions.** Class components stay class components; the established test pattern stays. Do not silently fork a new idiom.
12. **Fail loud.** "Completed successfully" while silently skipping records is the worst class of bug. Surface uncertainty and partial results; never hide them. (Mirrors the hooks' block-don't-ask design.)

**What compounds:** CLAUDE.md as institutional memory across sessions; eval-driven changes, not vibe-driven; checkpoints over speed; explicit conflicts over silent blending; discipline over the next framework; one repo, one rules file, no exceptions.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Do not commit secrets, credentials, PII, or live tokens.
2. Use environment variables for all secrets.
3. Never use `noreply@` sender addresses.
4. Never use Resend; email transport is Amazon SES (SMTP) only.
5. Never publish `.md` files in public-site folders (`dws10.com/`, `dws6.com/`, `onelifetime.world/`, and their `landing-pages/` mirrors).

9. Keep edits scoped; do not do unrelated refactors.
10. Use PowerShell-first command examples on Windows (`.ps1`, `.\script.ps1`).
11. **`gcloud` is a CMD-based tool, not PowerShell.** All `gcloud` examples MUST use CMD syntax — single-line OR caret (`^`) continuation, never backtick (`` ` ``). PowerShell-first (Rule 10) still applies for `.ps1` scripts and other Windows commands; the CMD rule is specific to `gcloud`. When a flow mixes `.ps1` and `gcloud`, invoke the `.ps1` via `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\script.ps1` from CMD rather than switching shells mid-flow. See `/gcr-skill`.
12. **Never lose document formulation data.** When rewriting or updating documents, preserve all eloquent formulations, philosophical passages, quotes, mottos, and cultural wisdom from earlier versions. A rewrite that strips these is destructive data loss. See `DWS_DOCUMENT_STANDARD.md` §21.
13. **Never publish a blog post the HIC has not read and approved.** ABSOLUTE. Every blog entry — any language, any site, any length, including translations, LSJ issues, and cron-drafted posts — requires a draft at `docs/blog-drafts/<slug>.md` whose full text was shown to the HIC **in one fenced code block**, and which reads `Status: APPROVED` before anything is published. Use `/blog-draft`. Show the text, then **stop and ask in that turn** — never draft and publish in one move. `Status: APPROVED` is flipped only on an explicit approval **about that post**; a general "go ahead", silence, or approval of something else is not approval. Enforced by `.claude/hooks/blog-draft-gate.sh`, but the rule binds whether or not the hook is armed — a bypass (generator, cron, fresh clone, unloaded hook) is not permission. ## Security Coding Rules

- No `exec()` with interpolated strings for shelling out; use safe argument-based execution.

### Secret Egress Rules (read AND write sides)

`Read`-tool deny rules only cover half the threat: the breach comes from a secret
being **written into a place nobody checks** (a committed file, a PR/issue body, a
log, an MCP call). Enforced by `.claude/hooks/{pretooluse-guard,secret-scan,secret-output-scan}.sh`;
follow them in spirit even where a hook does not yet reach:

- Never read secret material via Bash to pull it into context: no `cat`/`grep`/`head`/`tail`/`less`/`base64`/`strings` of `.env*` (except `.env.example`/`.sample`/`.template`), `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa`, or `*secret*`/`*credentials*` files. Use a specific non-secret env var if you truly need one value.
- Never run a bare environment dump (`env`, `printenv`) — it exposes every secret at once.
- If a secret value surfaces in command output (e.g. an error body, a DSN, a token), do **not** persist it: not into files, commits, PR/issue/review bodies, MCP tool arguments, logs, or docs. Reference it via `process.env` / an env var name instead.
- Secrets include more than provider-prefixed keys: DSNs with embedded creds (`******…`), bare JWTs, `Bearer` tokens, DB passwords, GPG passphrases, and OAuth client secrets all count.
- Do not rely on `settings.json` `deny` alone — it can be silently bypassed (e.g. the 50-subcommand parser cap); the hooks are the real enforcement layer.

## Skill Codification Rule ("Asked Twice = Failure")

No one-off judgment work. If the user asks for something that will need to happen again, the agent must:

1. Do it manually the first time on 3–10 items.
2. Show the output to the user.
3. If the user approves, codify it as a parameterized skill in `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (judgment work) or `.claude/commands/<name>.md` (slash-invocable workflow). If the task is deterministic and time-driven, also register a cron entry per the Script Automation Rule.
4. Re-run the new skill once to verify it reproduces the approved output.

**Test:** If the user has to ask for the same thing twice without it being a one-line skill invocation, the agent failed. Document repeating patterns in `SKILL.md` files, not in chat scrollback.

**Skill shape:** Skill files are parameterized procedures, not domain scripts. A skill describes the process; the invocation supplies the world (TARGET, KIND, DATASET, ROLE). Four near-identical skills with different filenames is a smell — collapse them into one skill with arguments.

**Learning loop:** Run `/learn SCOPE=last-week` after `/retro` (or at the end of a feature). It reads retros, commit churn, and hook audit logs, diarizes the mediocre outcomes ("OK but not great"), and emits a read-only edit plan in `docs/learning-loops/`. A human applies approved edits in a follow-up commit titled `learn: <scope> rule updates`. Skills get better; the harness stays thin.

**Keeping the HIC informed is a primary deliverable of every substantive session, not an afterthought.** New ideas, concepts, theories, code, whitepapers, and artifacts are welcome to build DWS further — but an artifact only a machine session ever saw dies in ephemeral container memory and no Human-In-Command (HIC) ever understood or authorized it. Canonical: `DWS_LEARNING_STANDARD.md`; stated as a canonical fact in `DWS_TRUTH_STANDARD.md` §2F + row 30. **Legal basis: EU AI Act Article 14 (human oversight)** — HIC = Human-In-Command is the DWS implementation.

Before ending a **substantive** session (new idea/code/artifact/signal/incident — see the standard's gate; trivial typo/dep/lookup sessions are exempt), produce the **HIC Learning Outcome — six-step minimum:**

1. **Update the knowledge base** (`kb/`, via `/kb`).
2. **Write a field note** (`docs/field-notes/YYYY-MM-DD-topic.md`).
3. **Add an HTML version into `Learn/`** (`scripts/render-doc.sh`; Document Standard §18).
4. **Export a copy to Drive** (repo stays source-of-truth — export without a repo source is a drift incident, §2E).
5. **Ask the HIC one real, decision-shaped question** — the Article 14 intervention point.
6. **Calendar every dated commitment** — every deadline, expiry, meeting, follow-up or renewal the session produced or discovered, put into Google Calendar in the session that found it (`Google_Calendar.create_event`). See `DWS_LEARNING_STANDARD.md` §4.1.

**Step 5 hands the HIC what to decide now; step 6 hands them what to act on later.** A date written only into a `.md` file will be missed — a document never reminds anyone. Calendar the **derived** dates too (a 3-month validity implies a follow-up date; a 3-month certificate implies a re-order date), give each event a title naming the consequence, the source file in the description, and a lead time matched to how long the action actually takes.

A skipped step must be recorded as `N/A — <reason>` in the field note (silent omission violates Rule 12, Fail Loud).

Score each gate 0–3: absent, claimed, demonstrated, independently validated. Passing requires no zero, production proof for Gates 1, 3, 6, 7, and 9, and at least 24/30.

## 6. Strategy loop

1. **Observe:** capture a real decision, outcome, failure, regulation, signal, or expert correction.
2. **Question:** formulate the decision question and competing hypotheses.
3. **Map:** bind roles, ontology, evidence, controls, and economic value.
4. **Evaluate first:** define gold cases, failure cases, baseline, threshold, and stop conditions.
5. **Run:** execute with claim-level evidence and uncertainty.
6. **HIC decision:** approve, override, request evidence, or stop.
7. **Measure:** record quality, cycle time, review effort, economic effect, MGD, and CRC.
8. **Learn:** convert approved learning into an evaluation case, ontology update, skill, policy, or threshold.
9. **Productize:** expose the capability through product, API/CLI, MCP, dashboard, and audit pack.
10. **Scale:** sell the proven decision to the next role, site, business unit, or industry.

Review failures weekly, prioritize by MGD/CRC monthly, gate every SKU quarterly, and independently reproduce Level 4–5 claims annually.

### Quarterly strategic review layer (adopted from external review, 05.08.2026 — see §13)

The ten steps above are the operational loop. Once per quarter, before the SKU
gating pass, answer five positioning questions in order; each answer must cite
Evidence Room artifacts, not intentions:

1. **Purpose** — why does an enterprise buyer pay for DWS IQ instead of a generic LLM wrapper or legacy GRC tool this quarter?
2. **Landscape** — where are incumbent tools currently failing on hallucination, reproducibility, or passive data collection, and which of those failures do we exploit?

### Adopted

| Gemini point                                                                                                             | Disposition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Five-question strategy cycle (Purpose → Landscape → Climate → Doctrine → Execution)                                      | Added to §6 as the quarterly strategic review layer. It is a positioning cycle; the 10-step loop remains the operational loop. They compose, they do not compete.                                                                                                                  |
| Deterministic carbon/ESG calculators "pass basic math, fail Post-Doc"                                                    | Correct and now explicit: deterministic calculators (Material Oracle, Emissions Data, `/carbon-analysis`) have a Level 3–4 ceiling in the §4 maturity model. Level 5 discovery (novel risk patterns, prospective validation) is their named upgrade path, not their current claim. |
| DGX pipeline enforcement — deterministic retrieval and proof-chain generation before any response reaches the user layer | Recorded as an implementation requirement for the 90-day programme (days 31–60, §10), aligned with KYA and Article 12 lineage.                                                                                                                                                     |

### Confirmed — already canon (no change)

- Benchmark definitions of doctorate/post-doctorate intelligence match the Executive decision in substance.
- "Unverified claims or un-cited outputs are blocked" = `DWS_TRUTH_STANDARD` row 35 + Product Gate 3.
- Generic Q&A chatbots and LLM wrappers failing both gates = the §8 "generic assistants requiring upgrade" list (`conversational-agent`, `firehorse-flow`).
- Ungrounded manual consulting failing the Doctorate gate = the §8 adoption-services reclassification.
- Passive regulatory news feeds failing both gates = why `/regulatory-radar` scores per-customer impact instead of aggregating headlines.

### Rejected — with reasons

| Gemini position                                                           | Why rejected                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Its "RQ Main" as the primary research question                            | Weaker duplicate of RQ0 (§2): no MGD/CRC measurability, no falsifiable hypothesis, no sovereignty/confidentiality/oversight constraints. RQ0 stays canonical.                       |
| "100% of outputs provide cryptographic- or audit-grade evidentiary proof" | Absolutist and unfalsifiable as a requirement. The scored gate (§5: 0–3 per gate, ≥24/30, production proof on Gates 1/3/6/7/9) is the enforceable form of the same intent.          |
| "Deprecate anything failing the Post-Doctorate gate"                      | Directly contradicts the HIC-approved Q1 decision: Level 3 is the approved flagship floor; Level 5 is the aspirational tier. Applying Gemini's rule would gut the approved catalog. |
| Category-level catalog exclusions as removal instructions                 | The approved removal scope is exactly the five SKUs in §12. Any further removal requires a new numbered HIC decision.                                                               |

## 14. Academic interlock — the four-year LUT doctorate as the external certifier

The doctorate-level claim in this strategy is not self-certified: the LUT PhD
programme (4 years, 2027–2030, supervision discussions with Prof. Kari
Smolander in progress) is the external mechanism that certifies it. Each DWS IQ
version supplies the production testbed that makes the research questions
falsifiable (DWS 7 customer evidence → Article I–II; DWS 8 carbon ledger →
Article II–III; the §5 Product Gate scores → Article III's measurement
instrument), and each peer-reviewed article becomes an Evidence Room artifact —
public, citable proof of Level 4 behavior that no marketing claim can
substitute. Full plan, year-by-year map, shared success scoreboard, and risk
controls: `docs/lut/dws-iq-phd-interlock-roadmap-2026-2030.md`.

3. Stanford HAI, 2025 AI Index — Responsible AI: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/responsible-ai
4. McKinsey, State of AI 2025: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai
5. European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Articles 12 and 14: https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-12 and https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14
6. OECD, AI in policy evaluation: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/governing-with-artificial-intelligence_795de142-en/full-report/ai-in-policy-evaluation_c88cc2fd.html

result.content:
line-by-line against this document. Per the surface-conflicts rule, each point is
adopted, confirmed as existing canon, or rejected with a reason — never blended.

### Adopted

| Gemini point                                                                                                             | Disposition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Five-question strategy cycle (Purpose → Landscape → Climate → Doctrine → Execution)                                      | Added to §6 as the quarterly strategic review layer. It is a positioning cycle; the 10-step loop remains the operational loop. They compose, they do not compete.                                                                                                                  |
| Deterministic carbon/ESG calculators "pass basic math, fail Post-Doc" | Correct only at the component level: a calculator is Level 0–2 by itself. Embedded within a governed decision workflow it can support Levels 3–4; Level 5 requires novel hypothesis generation and prospective validation beyond deterministic calculation. |

### Confirmed — already canon (no change)

- Benchmark definitions of doctorate/post-doctorate intelligence match the Executive decision in substance.
- Material claims without evidence are blocked = `DWS_TRUTH_STANDARD` row 35 + Product Gate 3.
- Generic Q&A chatbots and LLM wrappers failing both gates = the §8 "generic assistants requiring upgrade" list (`conversational-agent`, `firehorse-flow`).
- Ungrounded manual consulting failing the Doctorate gate = the §8 adoption-services reclassification.
- Passive regulatory news feeds failing both gates = why `/regulatory-radar` scores per-customer impact instead of aggregating headlines.

### Rejected — with reasons

| Gemini position                                                           | Why rejected                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Its "RQ Main" as the primary research question                            | Weaker duplicate of RQ0 (§2): no MGD/CRC measurability, no falsifiable hypothesis, no sovereignty/confidentiality/oversight constraints. RQ0 stays canonical.                       |
| "100% of outputs provide cryptographic- or audit-grade evidentiary proof" | Absolutist and unfalsifiable as a requirement. The scored gate (§5: 0–3 per gate, ≥24/30, production proof on Gates 1/3/6/7/9) is the enforceable form of the same intent.          |
| "Deterministic retrieval and proof-chain generation before any response" | Retrieval and model inference are not generally deterministic, and non-material output does not require a proof chain. DWS instead requires reconstructable audit replay and evidence for every material claim. |
| "Deprecate anything failing the Post-Doctorate gate"                      | Directly contradicts the HIC-approved Q1 decision: Level 3 is the approved flagship floor; Level 5 is the aspirational tier. Applying Gemini's rule would gut the approved catalog. |
| Category-level catalog exclusions as removal instructions                 | The approved removal scope is exactly the five SKUs in §12. Any further removal requires a new numbered HIC decision.                                                               |

## 14. Academic interlock — the four-year LUT doctorate as an external validation pathway

The doctorate-level claim in this strategy must not be self-certified. The LUT PhD
programme (4 years, 2027–2030, supervision discussions with Prof. Kari
Smolander in progress) can independently test and publish evidence relevant to it. Each DWS IQ
version supplies the production testbed that makes the research questions
falsifiable (DWS 7 customer evidence → Article I–II; DWS 8 carbon ledger →
Article II–III; the §5 Product Gate scores → Article III's measurement
instrument), and each peer-reviewed article can become an Evidence Room artifact —
public, citable evidence relevant to Level 4 behavior. Product-level claims still
require the independent reproduction and evaluation defined by the Product Gate. Full plan, year-by-year map, shared success scoreboard, and risk
controls: `docs/lut/dws-iq-phd-interlock-roadmap-2026-2030.md`.

## Sources

1. NIST AI RMF and Generative AI Profile: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework
2. Stanford HAI, 2025 AI Index — Economy: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/economy
3. Stanford HAI, 2025 AI Index — Responsible AI: https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/responsible-ai
4. McKinsey, State of AI 2025: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai
5. European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Articles 12 and 14: https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-12 and https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14
6. OECD, AI in policy evaluation: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/governing-with-artificial-intelligence_795de142-en/full-report/ai-in-policy-evaluation_c88cc2fd.html
7. Internal sources: `DWS_TRUTH_STANDARD.md`, `DWS_PRODUCT_STANDARD.md`, `DWS_MARKET_RESEARCH_STANDARD.md`, `DWS_ROLES_REGISTRY.md`, `AI_AGENT_GUIDELINES.md`, `config/truth/mgd-crc-metrics.json`, and `dws10.com/config/products.json`.

# DWS IQ × LUT PhD Interlock Roadmap 2026–2030

***

# VERSION AND AGENT HISTORY

Version: 1.0

Sessions & Modifications:

- Version: 1.0 | Tool: Claude Code | Session: session_01T3cDnVQrtyrBNvLT9KeyeW | Date: 05.08.2026 | Changes: Initial creation — four-year LUT doctorate mapped onto the DWS IQ 7→8→9 version roadmap; mutual-reinforcement plan (product supplies the testbed, doctorate supplies the proof); per-year article plan; success criteria and risks for both tracks. Anchored to Strategy_Loop.md v1.4 §14.

Document Status:

- Created: 05.08.2026
- Last Modified: 05.08.2026
- Language: English
- Languages Available: English
- Publication Status: DRAFT — planning document, pending supervisor alignment
- Document Type: Internal Roadmap / Academic-Product Interlock Plan
- Owner: Risto Anton Päärni, Founder, CEO, Lifetime Oy

***

## One sentence

The LUT doctorate (4 years, 2027–2030) and the DWS IQ version roadmap
(7 → 8 → 9, 2026–2031) are the same programme viewed from two sides: each DWS
version supplies the production testbed that makes the research questions
falsifiable, and each dissertation article can supply independent,
peer-reviewed evidence relevant to the product's Level 4 claims. The Product
Gate—not academic status—determines whether a product claim passes.

## Why the interlock wins on both causes

**Product → PhD (the testbed direction):**

- DWS 7's paying industrial customers (target: 16 by Q4 2027) are the empirical
  case base no competing doctoral candidate has — real MGD/CRC data, Article 12
  lineage, audit-grade decision records from regulated EU industry.
- The Strategy Loop's own discipline ("independently reproduce Level 4–5 claims
  annually", `Strategy_Loop.md` §6) _is_ an academic validation cycle — the
  doctorate makes it externally credentialed instead of self-run.
- KYA's four falsifiability gates (`standards/kya-open/SPEC.md` §0.6) cannot be
  cleared by Lifetime Oy alone by design. The university channel is the realistic
  source of gate #1 (independent implementations built by parties with no
  commercial relationship) and gate #2 (a conformance suite an implementation
  can fail, built as reviewed research instrumentation).

**PhD → Product (the proof direction):**

- Peer-reviewed articles become first-class Evidence Room artifacts
  (`Strategy_Loop.md` §7): a published, citable answer to "why is this
  doctorate-level?" that any enterprise buyer — R03/R04 research leaders,
  R13/R15 technical approvers — can verify without trusting our own materials.
- The §4 intelligence maturity model's Level 4 requires independent
  reproduction, adversarial review, and an expert baseline. Doctoral research can
  contribute evidence to those tests, but it does not certify the product or
  replace an independent Product Gate review.
- Enrolled doctoral status unlocks funding lanes closed to a plain company:
  Finnish foundations requiring a supervisor statement, Business Finland
  research tracks, EU instruments with academic-partner requirements
  (`docs/lut/fundraising-roadmap-2026-2027.md`, `docs/lut/fi-se-lanes-research-2026-07.md`).

## The four-year map

LUT industrial doctorate, part-time alongside the CEO role, article-based
dissertation (target: 4 publications + kappa). Supervision discussions with
Prof. Kari Smolander are in progress; the RQ set is in his inbox (lock rule:
changes to it are an external act requiring a HIC decision — PR #1745).

| Year             | LUT PhD track                                                                                                                                                                    | DWS IQ track                                                                                                                                     | The interlock deliverable                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Y0 · 2026 H2** | Supervision agreement; enrollment application; live funding windows (Liikesivistysrahasto closes 15.8.2026, Nokia Foundation 3.8–15.9.2026 — both need the supervisor statement) | DWS 7 Phase 2 execution; Q1-approved Intelligence Product Gate rollout from Q4 2026; first three evaluated decision workflows (90-day programme) | Research plan finalized against the _running_ testbed; the three gold-case decision workflows double as the dissertation's baseline datasets           |
| **Y1 · 2027**    | Enrollment + Article I: runtime assurance / KYA governance evidence from production (design-science method)                                                                      | DWS 7 GA push → 16 paying customers, €72K MRR target, ISO 27001                                                                                  | Article I's empirical section = DWS 7 pilot evidence; the article's method section = the reproducibility protocol the Evidence Room ships to customers |
| **Y2 · 2028**    | Article II: cross-industry ontology / carbon-ledger intelligence — what single-vertical tools cannot produce                                                                     | DWS 8 start: double-entry carbon ledger, 18-source data mesh, cross-vertical network effects                                                     | DWS 8's multi-customer ledger is Article II's dataset; Article II's review process pressure-tests the ledger's evidence claims before auditors do      |
| **Y3 · 2029**    | Article III: multi-vertical evaluation — cost-of-safety curves, calibration, human-override rates across industries                                                              | DWS 8 GA (Q4 2029); Phase 3B post-quantum foundation                                                                                             | The §5 Product Gate scores (0–3, ≥24/30) become Article III's measurement instrument — the catalog audit _is_ the study                                |
| **Y4 · 2030**    | Article IV + kappa; pre-examination; defense target end-2030/early-2031                                                                                                          | DWS 9 start: post-quantum sovereign platform, q-day-gated                                                                                        | Defense may add independent published evidence about versions 7–8; DWS 9 claims remain subject to their own Product Gate evidence                |

## Success criteria — both tracks, one scoreboard

The strategy works when each row is true on _both_ sides; a row true on one
side only is a drift warning:

| Signal                                     | PhD side                                           | Product side                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Falsifiable evidence                       | Article accepted at peer review                    | Same evidence pack passes a customer/auditor review (MGD counted, Article 12 lineage intact)        |
| Independent validation                     | External co-authors / reviewers reproduce results  | KYA gate #1–#2 progress: an implementation not built by Lifetime, a conformance suite that can fail |
| Knowledge discovery (post-doctorate level) | A novel validated finding per dissertation article | ≥1 validated discovery per quarter changes an enterprise decision (`Strategy_Loop.md` §11)          |
| Funding                                    | Foundation grants + doctoral funding secured       | MRR growth carries the company without diluting for research time                                   |

## Risks and their controls

1. **Over-scoping** — the dominant failure mode named by the supervisory review
   (PR #1712). Control: articles map 1:1 to already-planned DWS version
   deliverables; no article requires work the product roadmap doesn't fund.
2. **Founder bandwidth** (CEO + doctorate). Control: the interlock is designed
   so the same artifact serves both sides once — evidence packs, evaluation
   runs, and gate audits are produced for customers and _reused_ in articles,
   never duplicated.
3. **Funding window misses.** Both live 2026 windows require the supervisor
   statement — the critical path is the Smolander working session, not the
   writing. Next windows otherwise fall to 2027 (`docs/lut/fi-se-lanes-research-2026-07.md`).
4. **Thesis-lock discipline.** The RQ set sits in the supervisor's inbox;
   revisions are RED-zone (HIC + external act). This roadmap deliberately cites
   RQs by role (assurance / ontology / evaluation) rather than renumbering them.
5. **DWS 9 slippage is acceptable; Y4 is not coupled to it.** The defense
   depends on Articles I–III evidence from versions 7–8 only; DWS 9 timing is
   q-day-gated by design and the dissertation must not wait on it.

## Standing references

- Version roadmaps: `DWS7_ROADMAP.md` (Q1 2026–Q4 2027), `DWS8_ROADMAP.md`
  (Q1 2028–Q4 2029), `DWS9_ROADMAP.md` (2030+, q-day-gated), `AEGIS_ROADMAP.md`
- Strategy: `Strategy_Loop.md` v1.4 (RQ0, maturity model, Product Gate, §13 external-review reconciliation, §14 pointer here)
- PhD corpus: `docs/PHD_FIREHORSE_EN.md` §1.2 (seven RQs), §14.42 (four-gate falsifiability); PR #1712 (supervisory review), PR #1745 (falsifiability audit)
- Funding: `docs/lut/fundraising-roadmap-2026-2027.md`, `docs/lut/docs/lut/fi-se-lanes-research-2026-07.md`
- Scope split rule: implementation evidence → master's thesis; market signals and scientific framing → PhD (CLAUDE.md Thesis Content Scope Rule). This document is a _planning_ artifact, not thesis content — nothing here edits the four thesis files.

Use the ask_user tool to ask the user clarifying questions when needed.

**IMPORTANT: Never ask questions via plain text output.** When you need input from the user, use this tool instead of asking in your response text. The tool provides a better UX and ensures the user's answer is captured properly.

Guidelines:
- Prefer multiple choice (provide choices array) over freeform for faster UX
- Do NOT include "Other", "Something else", or similar catch-all choices - the UI automatically adds a freeform input option
- Only use pure freeform (no choices) when the answer truly cannot be predicted
- Ask one question at a time - do not batch multiple questions
- Don't ask the questions in bullet points or numbered lists. Ask each question in a clear sentence or paragraph form.
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first choice and add "(Recommended)" to the label
  Example: choices: ["PostgreSQL (Recommended)", "MySQL", "SQLite"]

Examples:
1. BAD - bundling multiple questions into one and asking the user to confirm or break them apart:
  { "question": "Here's what I'm thinking:\n1. Use PostgreSQL for the database\n2. Add Redis for caching\n3. Use JWT for auth\nDoes this sound good, or would you like to discuss each choice individually?", "choices": ["Sounds good", "Let's discuss individually"] }
  WORKAROUND - ask one focused question per tool call:
  First call:  { "question": "What database should I use?", "choices": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"] }
  Second call: { "question": "Should I add Redis for caching?", "choices": ["Yes", "No"] }
  Third call:  { "question": "What auth strategy should I use?", "choices": ["JWT", "Session-based", "OAuth"] }
2. BAD - embedding choices in the question text instead of using the choices field:
  { "question": "What database should I use? (PostgreSQL, MySQL, or SQLite)" }
  WORKAROUND - put the options in the choices array:
  { "question": "What database should I use?", "choices": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"] }

When to STOP and ask (do not assume):
- Design decisions that significantly affect implementation approach
- Behavioral questions (e.g., "should this be unlimited or capped?")
- Scope ambiguity (e.g., which features to include/exclude)
- Edge cases where multiple reasonable approaches exist

<sql>
**Session database** (database: "session", the default):
The per-session database persists across the session but is isolated from other sessions.

Use SQL for structured operational data such as todo lists, test cases, batch items, and session state.

**Pre-existing tables (ready to use):**
- `todos`: id, title, description, status (pending/in_progress/done/blocked), created_at, updated_at
- `todo_deps`: todo_id, depends_on (for dependency tracking)

**Todo tracking:**
Use descriptive kebab-case IDs (not t1, t2). Write titles in gerund form (e.g. "Creating user auth module"). Include enough detail that the todo can be executed without referring back to the plan:
```sql
INSERT INTO todos (id, title, description) VALUES
  ('user-auth', 'Creating user auth module', 'Implement JWT auth in src/auth/ so login, logout, and token refresh don''t depend on server sessions. Use bcrypt for password hashing.');
```

**Todo status:**
- `pending`: Todo is waiting to be started
- `in_progress`: You are actively working on this todo (set this before starting!)
- `done`: Todo is complete
- `blocked`: Todo cannot proceed (document why in description)

**Dependencies:** Insert into todo_deps when one todo must complete before another:
```sql
INSERT INTO todo_deps (todo_id, depends_on) VALUES ('api-routes', 'user-model');  -- routes wait for model
```

**Create any tables you need.** The database is yours to use for any purpose:
- Load and query data (CSVs, API responses, file listings)
- Store intermediate results for structured multi-step work
- Query any workflow data that benefits from SQL

Common patterns:

1. **Todo tracking with dependencies:**
```sql
-- todos and todo_deps already exist — do NOT CREATE them, just INSERT:
INSERT INTO todos (id, title, description) VALUES ('user-model', 'Creating user model', 'Define the User schema and relations in src/models/user.ts');

-- Find todos with no pending dependencies ("ready" query):
SELECT t.* FROM todos t
WHERE t.status = 'pending'
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM todo_deps td
    JOIN todos dep ON td.depends_on = dep.id
    WHERE td.todo_id = t.id AND dep.status != 'done'
);
```

2. **Session state (key-value):**
```sql
CREATE TABLE session_state (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT);
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO session_state (key, value) VALUES ('current_phase', 'testing');
SELECT value FROM session_state WHERE key = 'current_phase';
```
</sql>

This repo uses a fully automated multi-agent PR workflow that **replaces manual human-in-the-loop review**.

### Flow
1. **Claude Code** generates implementation on a feature branch and opens a draft PR
2. **AI Code Review (HIL)** workflow triggers automatically (`.github/workflows/ai-pr-review.yml`)
   - **Claude** does quick sanity check (security, correctness, breaking changes)
   - **Gemini** does deep HIL review (replaces human reviewer: edge cases, tests, architecture, security audit)
   - Both must approve — Gemini is the mandatory quality gate
   - Posts combined review as PR comment
   - Adds labels: `ai-reviewed` + `ai-approved` or `ai-changes-requested`
3. **If changes requested** (mandatory, not optional): Gemini's required changes + test gaps are formatted as structured @copilot instructions
   - Copilot coding agent picks up the comment and implements fixes autonomously
   - Pushes to the PR branch, re-triggering the review workflow
   - Loop repeats until both reviewers approve (typically 1-3 iterations)
4. **Gemini requests fixes → Copilot implements** (mandatory, not optional): This is the core automation loop
   - Gemini acts as strict senior engineer — flags critical issues, missing tests, edge cases
   - Fix instructions are specific and actionable (file:line references)
   - Copilot implements changes, runs `npm run build` and `npm test`
   - Review re-triggers automatically on push
5. **When approved**: `ai-approved` label triggers auto-merge workflow
   - Verifies all CI checks pass
   - Enables squash auto-merge (or adds `ready-to-merge` label)
6. **Human override**: Add `do-not-merge` or `needs-human-review` labels to pause

## 2. Lifetime Scope Signals Protocol

### What Are Lifetime Scope Signals?

Signals are the communication mechanism between agents. When an agent completes a milestone, it **emits** a signal. Other agents **listen** for signals before proceeding with dependent tasks.

### Signal Format

```
[AGENT-XX]:SIGNAL_TYPE:MILESTONE:TIMESTAMP
```

**Components:**

- `AGENT-XX`: Agent identifier (e.g., `AGENT-01`, `AGENT-07`)
- `SIGNAL_TYPE`: `READY`, `COMPLETE`, `ERROR`, `BLOCKED`
- `MILESTONE`: Specific deliverable (e.g., `supabase-auth`, `rls-policies`)
- `TIMESTAMP`: ISO 8601 format

**Examples:**

```
[AGENT-07]:READY:rls-policies:2026-01-05T14:30:00Z
[AGENT-01]:COMPLETE:v1-auth:2026-01-10T09:00:00Z
[AGENT-02]:BLOCKED:report-api:2026-01-06T10:15:00Z
```

### Signal Types

| Type       | Meaning                                          | Action                               |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `READY`    | Milestone achieved, dependent agents can proceed | Unblocks downstream agents           |
| `COMPLETE` | All agent work finished                          | Agent moves to complete status       |
| `ERROR`    | Agent encountered failure                        | Alerts coordinator, may block others |
| `BLOCKED`  | Agent waiting for external dependency            | No action until unblocked            |

### How Agents Learn Signals

#### Option A: File-Based (Current Implementation)

Agents read from `AGENT_SIGNAL_REGISTRY.json`:

```javascript
// coordinator.cjs
const registry = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("AGENT_SIGNAL_REGISTRY.json"));
const myDependencies = registry.agents["agent-02"].signals.listening;
const emittedSignals = collectEmittedSignals(registry);
const unmet = myDependencies.filter((sig) => !emittedSignals.has(sig));
// If unmet.length === 0, agent can proceed
```

**Commands:**

```bash
cd .workflows/agents
node coordinator.cjs status    # Show all agent statuses
node coordinator.cjs signals   # Show signal log
node coordinator.cjs ready     # Show which agents can launch
node coordinator.cjs emit agent-07 READY:schema-users  # Emit signal
```

#### Option B: MCP Hub Real-Time (Future)

```python

async def emit_signal(agent_id: str, signal: str):
    await supabase.table("agent_signals").insert({...})
    await notify_listeners(agent_id, signal)
```
